Towards Pensieve: Evaluating kn-graphRAG-starter and Long-Context Reasoning Approaches
Overview of kn-graphRAG-starter Architecture and Design
The kn-graphRAG-starter project is a local-first knowledge ingestion and retrieval pipeline, notable for its modular architecture and plugin-driven design. It operates as a sidecar knowledge base: all processed data (chunks, embeddings, graphs, summaries) reside in a dedicated .knowledge directory, leaving source documents untouched. Core components are cleanly separated into a library (kn for logic and data structures), executable scripts (bin for CLI tasks), and attribute plugins (plugins for pluggable data enrichment tasks). This separation makes the system easy to maintain and extend, as new plugins or tools can be added without breaking the core pipeline. The project implements a hybrid GraphRAG approach, combining two complementary knowledge structures:
Index-Based GraphRAG: It uses community-detection (Louvain via NetworkX) on term co-occurrence to form topic clusters, then generates summaries of each cluster. The result is a high-level topical index graph of the corpus. This index serves as a hierarchy of topics (similar to approaches like RAPTOR or ArchRAG) that guide coarse-grained retrieval and summarization.
Knowledge-Based GraphRAG: In parallel, it builds a fine-grained knowledge graph of entities by linking document chunks that share named entities (currently using regex-based extraction for nave entities). This yields an untyped co-occurrence graph capturing relationships between concepts or terms across the corpus. While primitive (no semantic types or labeled relations yet), this graph enables entity-level connections and multi-hop lookup of related information.
Retrieval Mechanism: The system supports hybrid retrieval: dense vector search (FAISSHNSW) augmented by BM25 keyword search. Queries are answered by retrieving top-matching chunks (and any relevant community summaries) and prepending them to the LLM prompt (a basic in-context augmentation). This ensures relevant context is given to the LLM for answer generation. However, the current retrieval doesnt fully exploit graph structure (e.g. it doesnt yet traverse the knowledge graph for multi-hop queries). Dashboard and Pipeline Orchestration: A recent addition is a web dashboard that visualizes the knowledge base and manages the ingestion pipeline. Users can enqueue ingestion jobs (document parsing, chunking, embedding, summarization) and monitor progress via a SQLite-backed job queue. The design documents (DESIGN.md and DESIGN_additions.md) outline advanced pipeline features like Corrective RAG (self-grading retriever feedback), hierarchical summarization (map-reduce style chunk-document-corpus summaries), and multi-source ingestion support. Many of these are planned as new modules (e.g. kncrag.py for corrective RAG, a sources adapter framework for diverse data, etc.) and integrate with the plugin system for extensibility. In summary, kn-graphRAG-starter provides a strong foundation: it is already a dashboard-driven pipeline for content ingestion, enrichment, and retrieval with excellent modularity and a clear path for growth. Its hybrid graph approach and plugin architecture align well with state-of-the-art GraphRAG concepts, albeit in early form. The next question is how suitable this base is for Pensieve an AIs long-term memory system requiring unbounded context reasoning beyond the limits of a static pipeline.
Suitability as the Foundation for Pensieve (Long-Term Memory System)
Pensieve is envisioned as a long-term memory module allowing an AI agent to reason over unbounded context effectively overcoming context window limits and knowledge rot by dynamically retrieving, aggregating, and reasoning over vast information stores. The kn-graphRAG-starter project offers many useful building blocks for this vision, but also faces key scalability and reasoning challenges under long-context scenarios:
Strengths of kn-graphRAG-starter: The projects hybrid graph index provides multi-granular organization of knowledge (topics vs. entities), which is crucial for navigating large corpora. Its local-first design and job queue can scale to ingest large data volumes and keep a persistent knowledge store on disk. The modular plugin system means we can iteratively add new capabilities (e.g. better entity extraction, new retrieval algorithms) without reworking the entire system. Also, by storing intermediate results (embeddings, summaries, graphs) in .knowledge, it avoids re-computation and allows fast lookups an advantage for long-term memory usage.
Limitations: In its current form, kn-graphRAG operates as a fixed pipeline queries follow a preset sequence (search - retrieve top-k chunks - prompt LLM). This static approach may falter on complex queries that require iterative exploration or multi-hop reasoning across many documents. Simply increasing the LLMs context size is not a panacea, as the OOLONG benchmark shows (even very large models struggle to utilize extremely long contexts effectively)
openreview.net
. Pensieve demands a more flexible, adaptive strategy where the system can break down queries, search in stages, and combine findings essentially doing meta-reasoning about how to use its knowledge.
Unbounded Context Handling: The current system still ultimately feeds a limited context window to the LLM (even if that window is, say, 4K or 16K tokens of retrieved text). To enable true long-term memory, Pensieve must allow reasoning over collections that far exceed any single prompt. This points to a need for an agentic orchestration approach: instead of one giant prompt, use the LLM to orchestrate multiple smaller retrieval and summarization steps. The design docs hint at this via map-reduce summarization and an upcoming knorchestrator.py for dynamic pipeline selection, but a more radical architectural shift may be needed to fully realize unbounded reasoning.
In short, kn-graphRAG-starter is an excellent foundation it provides the storage, indexing, and retrieval primitives required for a long-term memory. However, to become Pensieve, it should evolve from a static pipeline into an interactive reasoning system. The emerging concept of Recursive Language Models (RLMs) directly addresses this need by transforming the pipeline into a set of tools that a top-level LLM can call as needed. In the next sections, we compare this approach and others from recent research, to identify how Pensieve can achieve infinite context reasoning.
Insights from Recent Long-Context Reasoning Research
To chart the path forward for Pensieve, its instructive to examine complementary approaches and benchmarks that tackle long contexts and complex reasoning. Three notable references are:
OOLONG (ICLR 2026) a benchmark for long-context reasoning and aggregation tasks.
BrowseComp-Plus (arXiv 2025) a fixed-corpus benchmark for deep research agents with separate evaluation of retrievers and LLM reasoning.
Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) a lightweight neural model using recursive reasoning that outperforms large LLMs on puzzle-like tasks.
Each sheds light on limitations of current systems and offers ideas to extend or reshape Pensieve.
OOLONG: Long-Context Aggregation Challenges
Figure: OOLONG tasks require analyzing many chunks of information and aggregating results to answer a query. Standard LLMs show sharply degrading performance as context length grows, highlighting the need for smarter strategies beyond naive long-context usage. (Source: Oolong benchmark, ICLR 2026) OOLONG is a benchmark specifically designed to test whether models can utilize extremely large context (tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens) for reasoning
openreview.net
openreview.net
. Unlike simpler long-context tasks that just retrieve a single relevant passage, OOLONG questions require scanning many pieces of information and combining their insights to answer (for example, counting occurrences of a pattern across dozens of documents). It comprises Oolong-synth (synthetic data with controllable difficulty) and Oolong-real (real-world conversational data requiring temporal and relational reasoning)
openreview.net
. Crucially, nearly all tokens in the context are needed (not just filler), so models must truly read and aggregate, not just ignore irrelevant text. The findings from OOLONG are sobering: even state-of-the-art LLMs struggle. The best model tested (GPT-5, presumably a frontier model) achieved 50 accuracy at 128K tokens context
openreview.net
. Models often run out of context or get overwhelmed by the volume of data, exhibiting failures like incomplete reasoning traces and early termination of answers
openreview.net
openreview.net
. Performance degrades as context length increases, indicating current models dont scale well simply by having longer windows
openreview.net
. In essence, longer context alone isnt enough models need better ways to aggregate information. Implications for Pensieve: OOLONG highlights the aggregation problem: how to process a huge knowledge base and synthesize an answer from myriad pieces. A promising solution, demonstrated by the RLM approach, is to apply a divide-and-conquer strategy. Instead of stuffing 100K tokens into one prompt, an RLM will partition the context into manageable chunks, ask an LLM to analyze each chunk (e.g. classify or extract something), then aggregate those intermediate results. This is essentially a map-reduce executed by LLM agents. Notably, the RLM paper reports that an RLM using GPT-5-mini (a smaller model) outperformed GPT-5 by 34 points on a long OOLONG task (132K tokens) by using this recursive strategy. Pensieve can leverage this insight by enabling such recursive querying: treat the entire knowledge base as unbounded context that the system can slice into parts, analyze individually, and then combine. In practical terms, this means giving the AI tools to iterate over chunks (or graph sub-regions) and build an answer step-by-step exactly the capability an RLM-based architecture would provide.
BrowseComp-Plus: Deep Research and RetrieverLLM Synergy
While OOLONG stresses long single-document contexts, BrowseComp-Plus evaluates complex multi-document search and reasoning in a controlled setting. It is an improvement over the original BrowseComp benchmark: instead of using live web search (which is unpredictable and opaque), BrowseComp-Plus provides a fixed corpus with known relevant documents and hard negatives for each query
arxiv.org
. This allows precise measurement of how well an agent can perform deep research i.e. iterative search and multi-hop question answering when both the retrieval quality and the LLMs reasoning can be evaluated separately
arxiv.org
arxiv.org
. Key findings from BrowseComp-Plus demonstrate the importance of powerful retrievers and integrated reasoning. For example, a strong closed-book model alone is not enough: an open-source agent (Search-R1) with a basic BM25 retriever achieved only 3.86 accuracy, whereas GPT-5 (presumably with some built-in search capabilities or large knowledge) reached 55.9 on the same queries
arxiv.org
. But the best results came when a top LLM was paired with a top retriever GPT-5 combined with a high-quality embedding-based retriever (Qwen-Embedding-8B) scored 70.1 and did so with fewer search steps
arxiv.org
. This illustrates that retrieval is a critical component: a good retriever dramatically boosts performance by feeding the LLM the right information, and it can also reduce the number of iterations (the LLM doesnt have to search as many times if each search finds useful content). Implications for Pensieve: Pensieves design should emphasize a tight coupling of retrieval and reasoning. The kn-graphRAG base already has a hybrid retriever; to advance further, Pensieve could incorporate more graph-aware retrieval (e.g. follow edges in the knowledge graph to find related nodesdocuments) and even learned retrievers. A key idea from BrowseComp-Plus is to disentangle the LLM and the retrieval components for evaluation
arxiv.org
arxiv.org
in design, this means Pensieves architecture should allow swapping or upgrading the retriever independently of the LLM. For instance, Pensieve could support multiple retrieval modes: BM25, dense vector (Faiss), graph traversal, etc., and use whichever (or a combination) best fits the query type. The RLM paradigm naturally supports this: the LLM agent can decide at runtime whether to call a vector search function, do a graph neighbor lookup, or both, based on the question. This dynamic choice is analogous to GPT-5 picking a better retriever when available to improve accuracy
arxiv.org
. In sum, BrowseComp-Plus urges Pensieve to be a deep research agent able to perform multi-hop searches over a static knowledge repository and accurately integrate information from multiple sources. The tools-first design (LLM tools) will let us measure and improve each tool (retrievers, citation checking, etc.) separately, ensuring fairness and transparency in how Pensieve finds and uses information.
Tiny Recursive Model (TRM): Recursive Reasoning with Small Networks
Not all reasoning challenges are about huge text corpora; some are about complex problem-solving (logic puzzles, code analysis, etc.) that require intense step-by-step thinking. Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) offers an intriguing lesson: for certain tasks, a small, specialized model with the right recursive strategy can outperform massive LLMs
arxiv.org
reddit.com
. TRM, introduced in Less is More: Recursive Reasoning with Tiny Networks, is a 7-million-parameter model (just 2 transformer layers) that recursively calls itself to refine a solution. It was tested on challenging reasoning tasks like Sudoku, mazes, and the ARC-AGI reasoning benchmark. With only 0.01 of the parameters of giant models, TRM achieved 45 on ARC-AGI-1 and 8 on ARC-AGI-2 higher accuracy than most large LLMs like DeepSeek or Gemini 2.5B on those tasks
arxiv.org
. In other words, through iterative refinement, a tiny model thought its way to results that brute-force large models could not easily get. Implications for Pensieve: TRM showcases the power of micro-level recursion and suggests that Pensieves architecture should not rely solely on one big LLM for all reasoning. While the main Pensieve agent might be a powerful general LLM (for natural language understanding and broad knowledge), it could delegate specialized reasoning tasks to smaller, efficient models or algorithms. For example, if a users query or an intermediate step requires solving a complex puzzle, verifying a piece of code, or performing arithmeticlogic, Pensieve could invoke a tool or sub-module optimized for that (even a non-LLM algorithm or a tiny model like TRM). This not only can improve accuracy on those sub-tasks but is also computationally cheaper. The kn-graphRAG design already allows adding such tools as plugins. The RLM approach would treat a TRM solver as just another function the main LLM can call (e.g. solve_puzzle(subproblem) which internally uses the TRM model). Thus, Pensieve can fuse the TRM insight by adopting a heterogeneous model strategy: use large LLMs for broad reasoning and language tasks, but use recursive mini-models or deterministic methods for intensive reasoning that benefits from iterative refinement. This idea aligns with human cognition too where we sometimes write down intermediate steps or use scratch work (a small iterative process) to assist our main thought process. In summary, OOLONG and BrowseComp-Plus drive home the need for recursive, tool-augmented approaches to handle long or multi-step queries, and TRM demonstrates that recursion works at the algorithmic level as well. These insights point toward a more dynamic, integrated system for Pensieve, as discussed next.
Traditional vs. Advanced GraphRAG Paradigms for Long-Term Memory
Before formulating Pensieves design, its worth contextualizing it in terms of RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vs GraphRAG techniques. Traditional RAG systems use a simple retrieve-and-read loop, whereas GraphRAG systems introduce structured knowledge representations (graphs) to better navigate information
github.com
. Traditional RAG: The system indexes documents into a vector store or chunks, and at query time retrieves a handful of top-ranked chunks to feed the LLM. This approach is straightforward but has limitations: it doesnt inherently support multi-hop reasoning (each retrieval is independent) and can struggle when relevant information is scattered across many documents. GraphRAG: Augments RAG with a graph structure. Two common flavors were mentioned earlier:
Knowledge-based GraphRAG: Build a knowledge graph from the text (nodes are entities or concepts, edges are relations or co-occurrence). This yields fine-grained, explainable relationships. At query time, the system can traverse the graph to find related entities or facts, enabling multi-hop queries (e.g., find all papers cited by a given author, then retrieve those papers). Its great for domain-specific and relational queries
github.com
. The trade-off is that constructing a high-quality knowledge graph requires good entity recognition and relation extraction; if done navely, it may miss important links or include noisy ones. In Pensieves context, we plan to evolve the current co-occurrence graph into a true knowledge graph with typed entities and relations (using an LLM or NLP pipeline to extract triples). This will increase the expressiveness of the memory (e.g., one could query how does Concept X influence Y? and traverse the graph for answers).
Index-based GraphRAG: Build a hierarchical index of topics and subtopics (often via clustering and summarization)
github.com
. This provides a zoomed-out view of the knowledge base, which is useful for questions that require broad synthesis or exploration of a topic. In query processing, an index graph can help identify which section of the knowledge base is relevant before doing a deep dive. kn-graphRAGs Louvain communities are a first step in this direction. Pensieve can enhance this by generating multi-level summaries (sections - documents - clusters - entire corpus), so that even if asked for a high-level summary or comparison, it can use those pre-computed summaries instead of scanning everything from scratch. An advanced index-based technique is to allow the LLM to follow the index graph in a graph-of-thought manner effectively a guided chain-of-thought that hops between topic nodes.
Advanced GraphRAG innovations from the recent survey include graph-aware retrieval algorithms and structure-guided prompting
github.com
. For example, a graph-aware retriever might rank documents higher if they are graph-neighbors of known relevant nodes (implementing a form of semantic spreading activation or logical reasoning). Pensieve could use such a method: after an initial retrieval, fetch connected nodes in the knowledge graph to surface related info that a pure vector search might miss (this was hinted as a planned evolution in the design docs). Another innovation is prompting the LLM with the graph structure explicitly e.g., giving it chain-of-thought instructions like Use the following relations or providing it with a subgraph of relevant entities to incorporate. Graph-enhanced Chain-of-Thought (Graph-CoT) is one approach where the LLM is guided to reason along edges of the knowledge graph. Pensieve could employ Graph-CoT by, say, injecting the path of reasoning (from the graph) into the prompt or having the agent output which nodes its exploring as part of its answer trace. In designing Pensieve, we will blend these paradigms: the graph serves as both an index and a knowledge base, and the LLM-based agent will leverage it dynamically. The RLM-based Pensieve effectively treats GraphRAG components as tools rather than fixed stages. This means the system can achieve the benefits of GraphRAG (multi-hop reasoning, large-scale efficient retrieval) without hard-coding a single workflow. Instead, the LLM can choose to first do an index lookup, then a graph traversal, then a vector search on a narrowed subset, etc. whatever the problem demands. This flexible orchestration is the hallmark of the RLM approach, which we compare next.
Comparative Assessment of Approaches
To clarify the distinctions and complementary strengths of each discussed approach, the table below summarizes how they address long-term, unbounded memory and reasoning:
ApproachConcept	Core Idea	Strengths	Limitations
kn-graphRAG-starter (Pipeline)	Fixed pipeline (ingest embed graph retrieve answer) with hybrid graph index	- Solid modular foundation (plugins, queue, dashboard)
- Combines topical summaries and basic knowledge graph for context organization	- Static retrieval flow not adaptive to complex queries
- Limited exploitation of graph beyond simple links
- Bounded prompt context (no true infinite memory)
Traditional GraphRAG	Use knowledge graphs or index graphs to augment RAG pipelines	- Multi-hop reasoning via structured relations
github.com

- More interpretable answers (graphs provide rationale)	- Graph construction can be complex or error-prone
- Often still requires fixed pipeline logic (less flexible)
Recursive Language Model (RLM)	Treat the LLM as an agent in a REPL with tools (search, graph query, etc.); LLM decomposes queries and context recursively	- Unbounded context: can handle extremely large knowledge by iterative processing (no fixed context size)
- Adaptable strategy: chooses what tool or step to use next (better for complex or unexpected queries)
- Solves OOLONG-type tasks by map-reduce over context	- More complex to implement (needs sandbox, tool APIs, managing LLM code execution)
- May require many LLM calls, raising latency or compute costs (mitigated by using smaller LMs for sub-tasks)
BrowseComp-Plus Style	Fixed corpus, emphasis on retrievalLLM evaluation separately	- Highlights importance of strong retrievers (in Pensieve: motivates advanced search indices and graph queries)
arxiv.org

- Ensures reproducibility and tunability of the knowledge source (Pensieves .knowledge store plays this role)	- Benchmark, not an architecture; informs evaluation criteria more than design
- Assumes queries have a bounded relevant set (Pensieve must handle evolving KB over time)
Tiny Recursive Model (TRM)	7M param model that iteratively refines its output on a fixed task
arxiv.org
- Extraordinary efficiency on certain reasoning tasks (outperforms much larger models on puzzles)
arxiv.org

- Demonstrates value of recursion in reasoning (iteration can replace scale)	- Specialized to small, well-defined problems (not a general QA system)
- Needs integration into a larger system to be broadly useful (i.e. as a tool within RLM rather than standalone for Pensieve)
Pensieve (Target)	Fusion of the above: RLM-driven orchestration over GraphRAG knowledge base, plus specialized modules	- Can handle long-term knowledge without context limits (via RLM) and with rich relational understanding (via GraphRAG)
- Leverages best tool for each task: graph traversal for relations, vector search for similarity, mini-model for logic, etc.
- Learns and personalizes over time (possible with usage data guiding retrieval rankings)	- Will require careful engineering to coordinate many components (graph updates, indexes, LLM calls, etc.)
- Complex evaluation: success depends on interplay of retrieval, reasoning, and possibly learning user preferences
In essence, Pensieves approach will subsume the others: it aims to be an RLM-based system built on a GraphRAG knowledge foundation, augmented with recursive reasoning techniques. This combines the structured knowledge and efficient retrieval of GraphRAG with the flexibility and power of an LLM-agent that can orchestrate its own sequence of actions. It also keeps room for incorporating innovations like TRM as subroutines for intense reasoning tasks.
Architectural Design Trade-offs and Considerations
Designing Pensieve involves balancing several trade-offs:
Pipeline vs. Agentic Orchestration: A fixed pipeline (like traditional kn-graphRAG) is simpler and more deterministic, whereas an agentic RLM approach is more flexible but harder to predict and debug. Pensieve will lean towards the agentic side for capability reasons, but we must design robust safeguards (e.g., timeouts, cost limits, fallback behaviors) since an LLM given free rein to call tools could loop or choose suboptimal actions. The orchestration layer in Pensieve might combine both approaches: a high-level policy (possibly a simple pipeline for straightforward queries) and an RLM mode for complex ones.
Knowledge Graph Richness vs. Simplicity: A richer knowledge graph (with typed nodesedges, updated relations) provides more precise retrieval and reasoning (you can ask very specific queries like find all papers where Person X collaborated with Person Y). However, maintaining such a graph is challenging: it requires NLP pipelines or LLM prompts to extract entitiesrelations, and consistency must be managed as the knowledge base grows. We trade off precision vs. robustness: a simple co-occurrence graph is robust but imprecise; a rich semantic graph is precise but needs careful curation. A possible resolution is incremental sophistication: start with co-occurrence (already in kn-graphRAG), then gradually introduce typed relations for high-value entity types (people, organizations, important concepts).
Context Length vs. Summarization: Long-term memory systems can either try to cram ever more content into the prompt (with upcoming 100K token context models) or summarize and distill information. The trade-off is fidelity vs. feasibility: keeping raw text preserves all details (but is infeasible at large scale), whereas summarization loses detail but keeps context manageable. Pensieve should implement a hierarchy of summaries (as planned) and use on-demand retrieval of details. For example, Pensieve can store full text but only feed summaries to the LLM initially, with the ability to fetch the original text of a cited source if needed (perhaps as an LLM tool: get_document(doc_id)). This aligns with human memory: we remember gist and retrieve specifics when necessary.
Large LLM vs. Specialized Models: Relying on a single large LLM for everything simplifies design (just one model to interface with) but can be inefficient. Using specialized models (like a retrieval-optimized embedder, a fact-checker, TRM for puzzles) can improve performance and cost, but adds complexity in integration. Pensieve will pursue a hybrid: the primary interface remains a powerful generalist LLM (for understanding queries and overall reasoning), but behind the scenes it will invoke specialists when appropriate. This is already seen in RAG systems that use cross-encoders to re-rank passages or use a separate verifier model to check answers (similar to CRAGs self-grader). The RLM paradigm makes this more natural the agent can choose to call a specialist tool. We must ensure the intermediate outputs from these specialists are interpretable by the main LLM (likely via text or a standard format).
Static Knowledge Base vs. LearningAdaptive System: In a pure retrieval system, the knowledge base is static (documents in, answers out). But Pensieve, as a long-term memory, might observe which results were useful, which answers were good, and adapt over time. Theres a design decision between keeping it non-learning (no model fine-tuning, only improvements by adding data or adjusting prompts) vs. introducing learning (fine-tune LLM on feedback, train a reranker on click data, etc.). A near-term choice is to prioritize reliability (static system with user-controlled updates) and use lightweight learning for personalization scores or trust rankings. Over time, we can incorporate more learning, but carefully to avoid the system drifting or overwriting factual memory with user-specific bias.
Each of these trade-offs will be revisited as we build Pensieve. The architecture should be modular enough that we can adjust these dials (e.g., swap out the LLM for a bigger one if needed, plug in a learning-based component later, etc.) without reworking everything.
Opportunities for Fusion and Enhancement of Pensieve
Given all the inputs the existing kn-graphRAG system, the advanced methods from literature, and the design trade-offs we see several concrete opportunities to fuse ideas and enhance Pensieve beyond the sum of its parts:
RLM as the Core with GraphRAG Tools: The single most impactful change is to reframe the system as an RLM-centric architecture. Practically, this means developing a module that can take a user query and spawn a root LLM agent which has access to a suite of tools (search indices, graph queries, etc.). Existing kn-graphRAG components become those tools. For example, instead of a fixed retrieval step, we expose a function semantic_search(query) that the agent can call. Instead of always using the static summary of a cluster, the agent could call get_summary(topic_node) on demand. By doing this, Pensieve can dynamically decide how to answer: simple question? just do a direct search; complex aggregation? break it down into parts (map-reduce style); entity-centric query? traverse the knowledge graph first. This fusion addresses the unbounded context issue head-on: the LLM can iterate until its gathered enough info, rather than being limited by a single prompts worth of text.
Macro and Micro Recursion Together: We will integrate the macro-recursion of RLM (spawning sub-queries over large context) with micro-recursion inspired by TRM. Concretely, within the RLMs toolbox could be a function like solve_iteratively(problem_data) that is implemented by a tiny recursive model or a loop that uses the LLM on smaller pieces of the problem. For example, if asked to evaluate a complex logical condition or solve a puzzle embedded in the text, the main agent can hand it off to this solver. By fusing TRMs approach, Pensieve gains efficiency and accuracy on tasks that stump even large LLMs. This two-level recursion (RLM breaking down big context; TRM-style solving intense reasoning) could be a distinctive strength of Pensieve.
Enhanced Knowledge Graph Construction: We plan to upgrade the knowledge graph from a co-occurrence graph to a richer, semantic graph. Using an LLM itself as an annotation tool (via prompts asking it to extract triples from text) or existing NLP pipelines (for NER and relation extraction), Pensieve can populate the graph with typed entities (Person, Method, Term, etc.) and labeled relations (e.g., A cites B, X is part of Y). This would allow new types of queries and more precise multi-hop reasoning. For instance, Pensieve could understand a query like What are the key differences between approach X and Y in the literature? by following comparison or contrast relations in the graph. The project already envisioned an extract-entities-relations plugin for this; implementing that will be a priority. An advanced enhancement is to integrate a graph database or GNN for querying the graph at scale if needed (e.g., Neo4j or Deep Graph Library), though initially NetworkX in-memory may suffice for moderate sizes.
Hierarchical Memory and Summarization: Pensieve can implement a tiered memory: raw data at the bottom, various levels of summaries above. The map-reduce summarization in kn-graphRAG will be formalized so that every document has a summary, every cluster of documents has a meta-summary, and so on. These summaries themselves become part of the knowledge base (and could even be stored as special nodes in the graph). The agent can use these for quick overview responses or to decide where to focus. Additionally, by keeping older summaries and updating them as new information comes in, Pensieve can have an evolving long-term summary of a knowledge domain akin to a continuously refined wiki written by the AI. Summarization tools (possibly leveraging smaller LMs or open models for cost efficiency) will be integrated as background jobs in the pipeline and callable by the agent.
Personalization and Contextualization: In the long run, Pensieve as a personal long-term memory should tailor itself to the user. The original designs notion of trust and personalization scores can be woven in. For example, if a user tends to favor information from certain sources or has particular areas of interest, the retrieval function could weight those higher. The agent could maintain a profile (e.g., knowing that user is a software engineer, so coding-related answers can be more detailed). While this is peripheral to core long-context reasoning, it ensures the unbounded memory remains relevant and manageable (since truly unbounded knowledge can overwhelm if not filtered by user relevance). Modules like kntrust.py and knpersonalizer.py would handle these signals and could interface with the retrieval step (such as boosting or filtering results).
By fusing these elements, Pensieve moves toward a system that not only stores and retrieves information, but intelligently understands, organizes, and uses knowledge much like an expert research assistant.
Recommendations and Next Steps for Building Pensieve
To realize the vision of Pensieve, we propose the following concrete roadmap, broken into phases with key modules, dependencies, and milestones: Phase 1: Establish the RLM Orchestrator and Tool Interface (Immediate)
Goal: Replace the single-step query pipeline with an interactive agent loop.
Modules Actions:
RLM Core (knrlm.py): Implement the Recursive Language Model controller. This module will instantiate a sandboxed Python REPL environment and manage a dialog with the root LLM. Key tasks: feeding the LLM a system prompt describing available tools and the global context variable, receiving code-like plans from the LLM, executing them in the REPL (e.g. calling a search function), and returning results back to the LLM.
Tool APIs (knrepl_env.py): Develop the set of functions that the REPL will expose to the LLM. Initially include:
ctx a lazy-loaded object representing the entire knowledge base (all text chunks) that the LLM can iterate over if needed.
semantic_search(query, k) runs vector search on the chunks (requires integration with the FAISS or HNSW index in knretrieval.py).
keyword_search(query, k) runs BM25 keyword search (uses existing BM25 index).
get_neighbors(entity) retrieves nodes directly connected to a given entity in the knowledge graph (once graph is improved).
summarize(text) calls an LLM to summarize a given text (could use the same root LLM or a smaller model).
Basic Python utilities like print, len, regex (for filtering text via pattern matching), etc., to allow simple data processing by the LLM.
Dependencies: Use a Python sandbox library if needed for isolation (or restrict the REPLs available builtins for safety). Ensure the LLM gateway supports maintaining state between turns (the root LLM will have a conversation where it sees its previous commands and the results). This phase may rely on OpenAI function calling or output parsing to get structured actions from the LLM, or simpler prompt engineering to get it to output code.
Milestone: Demonstrate Hello World of RLM e.g., ask a question that requires reading a lot of text (like a question from OOLONG), and see the LLM agent autonomously loop over ctx and produce an answer. Success is the LLM can use semantic_search or chunk iteration in steps and produce a correct result that couldnt fit in a single prompt. Also ensure that for a simple factoid question, the LLM can answer directly with one search this tests that the agent can choose efficient paths (a regression check against the original pipelines ability).
Phase 2: Integrate Advanced GraphRAG Components (Next 12 months)
Goal: Inject the knowledge graph and hierarchical index capabilities into the RLM agent, and improve the knowledge organization.
Modules Actions:
Knowledge Graph Upgrade: Implement the extract_entities_relations plugin to populate a more semantic graph. This might use spaCy or Hugging Face models for NER, and an LLM prompt for relation extraction from sentences. Store the triples in a structured form (could be a JSON or a small SQLite table for relations). Update kngraph_nx.py to build a NetworkX graph with typed nodesedges from these triples.
Graph Tooling: Add functions to the REPL environment for graph-based retrieval:
graph.find(entity_name) to find nodes matching a name (helps the LLM find the exact entity node ID).
graph.neighbors(entity_id) (or a more semantic version like graph.query(pattern)) to traverse relations e.g., find all neighbors of a node or all nodes connected by a specific relation type. This allows multi-hop exploration via code (the LLM could loop calling graph.neighbors to walk the graph).
Possibly expose a graph.search(query) that uses the graph structure to aid retrieval e.g., find relevant entities via the graph then retrieve connected chunks. This could be an extension of the current retrieval that was planned to use graph neighbors.
Hierarchical Summaries: Finalize the map-reduce summarization feature. Implement jobs that create chunk summaries, then doc summaries from those, storing them in a new index (e.g., each summary can be treated as a pseudo-document). The REPL could have a get_summary(doc_id or topic_id) function to fetch these summaries on demand. This effectively gives the agent a fast way to get an overview of any part of the knowledge base. The index graph of topics may be integrated by linking summaries to graph nodes (if a topic cluster aligns with an entity or a community). Ensure the dashboard can display these summaries and their relations (for debugging and user insight).
Retriever Enhancements: Incorporate a stronger vector retriever model if available (for example, use a state-of-the-art embedding model like Qwen-Enc-8B as mentioned in BrowseComp-Plus
arxiv.org
). This might be optional due to resource constraints, but designing the retrieval interface to allow plugging in different embedding models will future-proof the system. Also, implement the Corrective RAG (CRAG) pipeline within the agents workflow: after an initial answer is drafted, the agent (or a separate critique function) can grade the answer against retrieved evidence and decide to iterate (re-retrieve or modify the query). This can be a tool like grade_answer(answer_text) that returns problematic claims or a score, prompting the agent to do another round of retrieval if needed.
Milestone: Graph-aware QA Ask a multi-hop question that specifically tests the knowledge graph, e.g., Find all papers that were co-authored by Person A and are about Topic B, and summarize what they conclude. A successful outcome would involve the agent using graph.find to get Person As node, graph.neighbors to traverse co-author relations or topic relations, retrieving the relevant papers, and summarizing them. This shows Pensieve can leverage structure not just keywords. Another milestone: run a sample from BrowseComp-Plus in a controlled way since that benchmark provides relevant documents, see if Pensieves agent can locate those documents in its corpus and answer with citations (this will validate the retrieverLLM synergy).
Phase 3: Scale and Personalize (3 months, ongoing)
Goal: Evolve Pensieve into a general-purpose, personalized knowledge engine with continuous learning.
Modules Actions:
Multi-Source Ingestion: Extend the ingestion pipeline to support diverse data sources beyond text files (e.g., web articles, PDFs, code repositories, emails). Implement source adapters as described in design docs. Each adapter will normalize content into the chunk document schema. This is important for Pensieve to truly be a long-term memory: it should ingest ongoing streams of data relevant to the user. For example, a GitHub adapter could allow Pensieve to ingest the users projects and answer questions about their own code with full context.
Continuous Update Mechanisms: Pensieve should handle updates gracefully new documents, changes, feedback. Implement a file watcher or scheduler that automatically processes new or updated files into the knowledge base (with versioning if needed). Also, capture user interactions: if the user corrects an answer or highlights a passage as important, feed that back into the system (perhaps via adjusting trustpersonalization scores).
Trust and Personalization: Activate the kntrust.py and knpersonalizer.py modules. Define a set of heuristics for trust (e.g., academic papers high trust, random web comments low trust, or use citation counts as a proxy) and for user relevance (e.g., if the user frequently opens documents on topic X, boost X-related content). Integrate these scores into retrieval ranking: for example, the semantic search function can weight the vector scores with a factor for TrustScore and PersonalRelevance, depending on user-selected mode (Objective vs Personalized results). Milestone here is the ability to toggle modes and see different answer behavior (like more emphasis on personal notes in personalized mode).
Evaluation Benchmarking: As Pensieve grows, institute regular evaluation on benchmarks like OOLONG and BrowseComp-Plus (or internal equivalents). This means building a test harness: given a set of long-context questions with known answers, measure Pensieves accuracy and the number of tool calls it uses, etc. This will quantify improvements and highlight remaining weaknesses (e.g., if it struggles with a certain relation type, we know to improve the graph in that area). We should also test on TRMs puzzle tasks to see if invoking a mini-model yields improvements on those specialized queries.
Milestone: User-facing Prototype Deliver a version of Pensieve accessible through the dashboard or a chat interface where a user can ask any question answerable from their knowledge base. The system should handle questions requiring deep context by engaging the RLM workflow under the hood, but from the user perspective its a seamless QA (with sources cited). This prototype should demonstrate the infinite memory aspect for instance, asking a question that requires information from 10 documents spread across the corpus, and getting a coherent answer that synthesizes them. A stretch goal is to enable a conversational continuity: the user can ask follow-ups and Pensieves agent keeps context from previous queries (since it can always look back at the conversation history stored as part of its knowledge).
By following this phased plan, we will progressively transform kn-graphRAG-starter into Pensieve, a powerful long-term memory system. Each phase builds on the last: first establishing the intelligent querying mechanism (RLM), then enriching the knowledge representations and tools (graph, summaries, retrievers), and finally scaling up to a continuous-learning, personalized assistant.
Conclusion
Pensieves journey is an ambitious fusion of retrieval-augmented generation, graph-based knowledge organization, and recursive reasoning. The kn-graphRAG-starter project gives us a solid launchpad with its modular pipeline and hybrid graph index, and the latest research OOLONG, BrowseComp-Plus, RLM, TRM lights the way to overcome the limitations of traditional systems. By adopting an RLM-centric architecture, Pensieve will treat the entirety of its knowledge base as accessible context, using an LLM brain to intelligently break down queries and traverse knowledge in pieces. GraphRAG principles ensure that knowledge is structured and navigable, enabling multi-hop and explainable reasoning, while techniques like TRM remind us that sometimes smaller iterative models can solve pieces of the puzzle more effectively than one giant leap. The end result we aim for is a long-term AI memory that can grow without bound yet remain accurate, efficient, and context-aware. It will not simply dump a 100,000-token document into a prompt and pray the model finds the answer; instead, it will orchestrate a symphony of searches, reads, and writes, much like a diligent researcher combing through an archive, taking notes, and forming a conclusion. This orchestrated approach directly addresses the unbounded context problem by decomposing the context itself allowing Pensieve to reason over far more information than any single models context window. In building Pensieve, we not only push the envelope of what an AI assistant can do with knowledge, but we also create a system that is extensible and evaluable. Each new tool or module (be it a better retriever, a new graph algorithm, or a reasoning micro-model) can plug into the agent and immediately lend its strengths. This modular, tool-augmented RLM environment is a promising paradigm for AI systems that must deal with ever-expanding knowledge. Pensieve will thus be at the forefront of infinite-context reasoning, turning the vision of an AI with a memory palace of knowledge into a practical reality. Sources:

1. What the Smol Training Playbook actually gives us
a. A clear stance: data curation architecture tweaks.

the-smol-training-playbook-the-...


b. Multi-stage pretraining mid-training is first-class.
They explicitly endorse: general pretraining midcontinued pretraining post-training, and they show that mid-training on a focused distribution (e.g. distilled reasoning) gives big jumps. the-smol-training-playbook-the-...

c. They already ran into the packed sequences are noisy problem and solved it with intra-document masking.
This is super relevant. They point out that most web docs are 2k tokens; if you just pack to 4k8k with standard causal masking, your tokens attend to unrelated documents, which hurts quality. Their fix: intra-document masking tokens can only look back inside their own doc. They also note PDFs are longer and help when mixed in. This is practically a smoking gun for us: if Pensieve is going to feed long, heterogenous chunks, we should mask by source by doc by graph-subtree.
the-smol-training-playbook-the-...

They hold the architecture fixed and vary the data: early stage broad, later stages higher quality more specialized (e.g. math, code, higher-quality versions of the same sets), and they even describe annealing ablations: 40 baseline 60 candidate data to see if the candidate deserves to be in the later stage. Thats exactly how we can test Pensieve-formatted corpora without restarting the world.
the-smol-training-playbook-the-...


e. They explicitly show a long-context training schedule: pretrain at 8k, then mid-train to 131k context on a smaller but targeted corpus. Thats the template for teach the model to stay coherent across very long sequences, but later.
the-smol-training-playbook-the-...

2. What it does not give us (and well have to supply)
No retrieval-aware graph-aware pretraining format.
They concatenate webcodemath and fix the mask; they dont talk about pretraining on retrieval sessions (query found nodes stitched context answer) or on explicit graph neighborhoods.

No indexable document layout.
Pensieve wants chunks that are born with stable IDs, relations, source lineage, and temporal position. The playbook is happy to shuffle and pack; it doesnt care about later replay.

No episodic user-centric memory stream.
Our problem involves a single humans selected context over time tweets, notes, saved posts, repos. The playbook is about general-web SOTA, not personal-corpus continuity.

So well take their procedure and swap in our data shapes.

ChatGPT said:
That actually makes life a lot easier

If we de-prioritize train our own model from scratch and instead say:

Pensieves job is to turn a messy, arbitrarily large pile of userwebreponotes into the best possible 1M-token (or smaller) context for some other LLM,

...then the center of gravity moves from modeling to organization distillation packing.

Heres how that shifts things.

1. New mission statement
Old: Teach the model to understand Pensieve-shaped data.
New: Make someone elses model feel like it has infinite memory by giving it only the right 0.1 of the data, in the right format, at the right time.

So Pensieve becomes an intelligence amplifier LLM prep chef, not a foundation-model lab.

2. What drops in priority
Big pretraining pipelines mostly gone. We dont need to buy the whole GPU farm.

Special Pensieve tokenization masking nice-to-have only if we do light finetuning.

Tiny recursive model as a learned component becomes optional; we can just call the LLM twice to get the same behavior most of the time.

We can still produce training data (for other peoples finetunes or our own small adapters), but the heavy recipe from the smol playbook becomes support tooling, not the product.

3. What rises in priority
We now care about 5 things:

Ingestion canonicalization
Get everything in, tag it, normalize it. Repos, PDFs, chats, web mirrors, notes. Keep provenance.

Multi-resolution distillation
For every unit of knowledge, keep:

raw source

local summary (13 paras)

ultra summary (13 sentences)

featuresmetadata (entities, time, source, topic)
Thats the pyramid. This is what lets you fill a 1M-token window with only what matters.

Relevance engine
Given a task, pick the right slices. This is a hybrid of:

fast textdense search

graph neighborhood expansion

query rewriting task decomposition

recency user-interest boosts

Session packer (this becomes the star)
Given: I want to talk to this model with 1M tokens, the packer decides:

which docs to include

which to include as summaries

which to include only as citationsIDs

in what order (global local evidence)

how to preserve threads (so the LLM can follow a chain)

Curationexport for finetune
Sometimes we do want to fine-tune an existing model to expect Pensieve layouts. Pensieve should output:

instructioncontextanswer triples

retrieval traces (I asked X I picked docs I answered Y)

contrastive pairs (relevant vs. distractor)
Thats data for training, not instead of training.

So the product is: Given N GB of chaos, give me the 1M-token best view for task T.

4. Architecture in this booster world
4.1 Keep the graphRAG core
Keep the .knowledge sidecar

Keep doc chunk entity community graph

Keep dashboard and job queue

Because we still need structure over big corpora.

4.2 Add a Context Planner (this is the new big piece)
This is the part the LLM talks to.

Inputs:

task description (user query, code question, debugging request...)

user profile recency

budget (e.g. you get 750k tokens max)

Steps:

Expand the task (LLM or rules): to do this I need background A, related work B, user files C, and raw evidence D.

For each needed thing, call retrievalgraph to get candidates.

Score and dedupe across all candidates (vector score, graph distance, source trust).

Select a resolution per item:

include raw (high importance, short)

include summary (high importance, long)

include titleID (low importance, maybe needed later)

Linearize into a single promptable document with section headings and markers:

Task
...
Global Background (auto)
...
User-Specific Context
...
Evidence (Cited)
...
Index of Omissions
...
Output:

final_context.txt 1M tokens

manifest.json (what was chosen, from where, at what resolution)

This is the thing you feed to GPT-o3, GPT-5, Qwen-VL-big, etc.

4.3 Retrieval stays modular
Because were not training our own base model, we can afford to use multiple retrievers in parallel:

BM25 keyword

dense (small open embeddings; or call an embedding API)

graph neighborhood

long doc skimmer (LLM ask: is this doc relevant?)

Then the planner merges those results.

4.4 Light finetuning thin wrappers only
Now it makes sense to do very small finetunes on top of someone elses model for things like:

Given a Pensieve manifest user query, auto-write the final prompt

Given a retrieved doc, produce the 3-level summary format we like

Given 5 candidate docs, rank by is this actually needed to answer?

Those are alignment routing tasks, not pretraining. We can train them on the data Pensieve itself generates.

5. How this affects the smol-playbook ideas
Intra-document masking still useful, but mostly if we create training data for these thin tasks. Not mission critical anymore.

Long-context mid-train we can just buy an LLM that already does 1M tokens and feed it our packed session. No need to do our own 8k131k run.

Data ablations still useful, but now its about does this curation scheme produce better prompts? not does it train a better base model?

So the playbook becomes a reference for how to evaluate data, not the thing we must implement.

6. What the system lifecycle looks like now
Ingest (everything)

Enrich (entities, graph, summaries, dedupe)

Store (chunked, multi-resolution)

Plan (given task, choose compress)

Serve (emit best-fit mega-context)

Optionally export (data for finetuning RLAIF router training)

No train 300B tokens from scratch step.

7. Limits and honest bits
We still cant truly give infinite context were just getting very good at choosing.

The hardest part becomes task understanding (what do I need to solve this?). Thats LLM-style reasoning, so we still want an LLM in the loop, but now as planner, not as target.

To make this actually good, we will want to collect telemetry (which chunks got used, which were ignored by the downstream LLM) and feed that back into the selector. Thats learning, but its tiny.

8. TL;DR shift
Before: Lets make a model that natively speaks Pensieve.

After: Lets make Pensieve a context OS for LLMs.

So the next work items become:

Finish ingestion graph summaries (you already have 70 in kn-graphRAG).

Build the Context Planner (LLM-orchestrated is fine).

Build the Session Packer with token-budgeting and multi-resolution.

Add exporters to spit out SFTranking datasets so, if later we want to fine-tune a helper model, we can.

That gets you an intelligence booster apparatus without touching big pretraining.

LLM calls Pensieve tool(s)

pensieve.search(user"warren", topic"RR2 zoning", k50)

pensieve.graph_expand(node"RR2", depth2)

pensieve.build_context(budget900000, purpose"compare_parcels")

Pensieve returns a structured context pack

high-level summaries

the exact PDF snippets

user notes

an index of stuff I didnt include because of budget

LLM looks at it
If its not enough (common in 1M-token cases), the LLM recurses:
Okay, give me the full zoning PDF too, but summarized by sections calls Pensieve again with a tighter query.

LLM answers user
(optionally citing context_pack.sources )

So we still get the good bits from the recursiveRLM papers:

LLM-directed tool use (LLM decides what to fetch next)

Multi-step refinement (LLM can say not enough, give me more in section 4.2)

Mapreduce style (LLM can ask for per-doc summaries, then ask Pensieve to merge)

But weve externalized the heavy lifting: Pensieve is the thing that knows how to do fast hybrid retrieval, graph hops, summarization tiers, token budgeting, and output in a promptable format.

You can think of it like this:

RLM brain
Pensieve memory pantry
LLM call flow go get me ingredients, Ill cook the answer.

So yes keep the recursive planners. Thats how you get adaptive context, not a single static retrieval. And it fits perfectly with the lower goal: we dont have to train a new model, we just give existing models a smarter, LLM-driven context feed.

Right. So, only concern now is the complexity of Pensieve tooling. How do we ensure each one of these tools is simple enough to be reliable while still useful for the LLM, and how many tools do we probably really need? What can we turn to for a comprehensive list of tools to start implementing, so we're not missing key ones, not creating poor tools that dont work in the ecosystem, and not overcomplicating any tool by relying on intelligence we dont have in the Pensieve app itself (e.g. can we do it all by relying on a local AI that only has some small amount of context or lower intelligence). Developing this list and figuring out which tools will be easy and difficult will matter a lot here
ChatGPT said:
Yep this is the right anxiety to have

If Pensieve turns into 50 half-baked tools the LLM has to guess how to use, itll fail. The trick is to make very few, very boring, very predictable tools and let the LLM do the clever part.

Heres a way to pin this down.

1. Design rules for Pensieve tools
One job each. Each tool should do one of: select, fetch, summarize, transform, or pack. Not 3 of those.

Deterministic smart. If it can be a SQL-ish filter or a BM25 query, do that instead of LLM-guessing. LLMs like reliable tools.

Tiny inputs. Even if Pensieve holds 200GB, tools should accept small JSON-y arguments strings, IDs, filters not the whole user corpus.

Stable schema. Always return items: , meta: ... or text: "...", sources: . LLMs tolerate low IQ better than they tolerate shape drift.

Composability. Every output should be a good input to another tool e.g. search fetch summarize pack.

LLM is the orchestrator, not the worker. Pensieve doesnt have to figure out relevance locally if a small model cant the LLM can ask for more and refine.

So: simple tools, smart planner.

2. How many tools do we actually need?
You can do a complete v1 with 812 tools.

Think in layers:

Layer A Core data access (34 tools)
These are the ones that must exist or nothing works.

search_text(query, k, filters?)

Deterministic: BM25 or simple dense.

Returns docchunk IDs snippets.

Easy.

get_docs(ids)

Fetch raw text markdown PDF-sliced text for specific IDs.

Should support give me just this page or section.

Easy.

list_related(id, kind"graph""thread""version")

Whats near this in the knowledge graph thread repo tree?

Basically graph-neighbors or conversation siblings.

Medium (needs graph built first).

get_summary(id, level123)

Returns precomputed summary (or lazy-computed if missing).

Medium (needs summarization pipeline).

That already gives the LLM superpowers: search fetch summarize compare.

Layer B Reducing to a context window (34 tools)
rank_for_task(task, candidates, budget)

Input: task string list of candidate IDs (from searchgraph) token budget.

Output: ordered list with suggested resolution (raw summary title-only).

This is the first smart-ish one but you can start with heuristic scoring (search score recency user tag) and add LLM rerank later.

Medium Hard (because its your quality valve).

pack_context(task, items, budget)

Turns ordered items into a single linear text (with headings, separators, source markers).

Purely deterministic.

Easy.

chunk_text(text, target_tokens)

For when the LLM says that PDF was too big, cut it.

Easy.

trace_context(items)

Returns a JSON manifest of what was included and why.

Easy.

Layer B is what makes Pensieve a context OS.

Layer C Convenience adapters (24 tools)
search_user_notes(query, k)

Same as search_text but pinned to user corpus.

Easy.

search_web_cached(query, k) (optional)

If you mirror web or have a news cache.

Medium.

summarize_on_demand(text, style)

LLM-backed, can be slow.

This is your ok do it live tool.

Medium (depends on local model).

extract_entities(text)

To grow the graph or let the LLM make a local subgraph.

Medium.

Thats it. 12 tools, tops. Most people ship with 57 first.

3. What to copy so we dont miss key ones
You asked what can we turn to for a comprehensive list, and there are basically three ecosystems worth mirroring:

OpenAI tools MCP style

search retrieve browse write-file read-file list-resources

We only need: search, retrieve, list, summarize

LangChain toolkits

Search docs, Load docs, Summarize, QA over docs, Code interpreter

The pattern is always: get narrow reduce answer

LlamaIndex query engines

Vector query, Graph query, Tree summarize, SQL query

We can just map those to our names.

So if we align our names schemas to those, every LLM thats been trained on tool-use examples will have a good prior.

4. Which ones are easy vs. hard
Easy (do first):

search_text (BM25, or local dense)

get_docs

pack_context

trace_context

chunk_text
all deterministic, no heavy AI needed.

Medium (needs infra or precompute):

get_summary (needs background summarization jobs)

list_related (needs a graph built)

search_user_notes (needs usersource filters)

summarize_on_demand (needs a local model, but can be small: 7B is fine)

Hard (quality-sensitive LLM-in-the-loop):

rank_for_task

because what is relevant is contextual

start with: score search_score 0.2recency 0.3user_boost

later add: call LLM to re-rank top 20

extract_entities (if you want high-quality, multi-language, domain-specific)

So your MVP can literally be: search fetch summarize pack.

5. Avoiding overcomplication intelligence we dont have
Key trick: make Pensieve tools non-opinionated and let the LLM ask again.

Example:

Tool returns 25 candidates but cant decide.

LLM: filter to only PDFs and user notes from 2024.

Tool: re-run with filters.

LLM: ok now pack context 400k tokens.

Because the LLM is the planner, Pensieve doesnt have to be very smart just very obedient.

And yes: you can do this all on a local AI thats only kinda smart (say, 7B13B) as long as:

it can summarize,

it can label relevance for a small candidate set (top 20),

and it can follow tool schemas.

If its too weak to plan multi-step, just let the remote or bigger LLM do the planning, and keep Pensieve local for data.

6. The final starter list
Heres a version you can drop into a repo as tools.md:

search_text(query, k20, filtersNone)

search_user(query, k20)

get_docs(ids, partsNone)

get_summary(id, level1)

list_related(id, mode"graph")

rank_for_task(task, candidates, budget_tokens)

pack_context(task, items, budget_tokens)

chunk_text(text, target_tokens)

summarize_on_demand(text, style"default")

trace_context(items)

Thats a clean 10. Ship 6 first.

So: yes to recursive planners, yes to LLM-directed tool use, no to tool bloat. Start with 6 deterministic tools, add 24 smart-ish ones once you see what the LLM actually asks for.

GraphRAG transforms unstructured text into structured knowledge graphs and uses these graphs to augment Large Language Model (LLM) outputs. It provides a framework for indexing and querying these knowledge graph memory structures.

The project helps connect information across diverse datasets, enabling answers to complex questions that traditional search methods often miss. It is suitable for domain-specific text data, supporting critical information discovery and analysis in noisy, mixed, or abstract datasets.

GraphRAG's functionality relies on a data pipeline that processes raw text through various stages to extract structured information. This process includes initial data ingestion, text chunking, and transformations to build the knowledge graph by identifying entities, relationships, and claims. The pipeline culminates in the creation of community reports and their embeddings. More details on this process are available in Data Pipeline and Transformation Suite.

The system creates and utilizes knowledge graph memory structures composed of entities, relationships, and communities. These structures are indexed and queried to enhance LLM outputs, allowing for storage, retrieval, and integration of structured memories into the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) process. These components work together to convert text into knowledge and then leverage that knowledge for various applications.
